items.title: How OpenEvidence scales medical search for 650K doctors
items.summary: OpenEvidence on VercelServes 650,000 doctors with medical searchCompletes production deployments in about five minutesAbsorbs traffic spikes without additional capacity provisioningReduced serverless spend by 90% with Fluid computeUpdates doctor- and patient-facing applications independently helps physicians find medical evidence during care, whether they’re checking a dosage on intensive care rounds or handling a case outside their specialty without a specialist nearby. Answers draw on peer-reviewed literature and include citations, so doctors can examine the sources behind them.OpenEvidenceOpenEvidence’s small team began using Vercel to get early experiments online and kept that workflow as the product grew, relying on the platform to handle web deployments and capacity.The stakes are different when software helps inform medical decisions. An incorrect answer can affect how a doctor treats a patient, while an unavailable application can cut off access to evidence when it is needed.OpenEvidence supported . The company also reported that .more than 20 million clinical consultations in January 2026more than 100 million Americans were treated by doctors using OpenEvidence in 2025"Honestly, life or death is not inaccurate," says Kush Khosla, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. "We operate in situations where it's an ER and they really need to know what's going on. Uptime is very, very important to us.""A lot of doctors and medical professionals are used to really outdated software," says Andy Yoon, Engineering Lead at OpenEvidence. A more modern experience still needs to meet physicians' expectations of speed, stability, clarity, and information they can trust. The small team needs a way to test updates to the web application before putting them into production and to roll back if something goes wrong.Andy recalls why Vercel suited the team he joined at OpenEvidence. "I was pretty much the only engineer on our team coming from an actual frontend background," he says. "Most of our team works in Python and machine learning." He adds, "Given the makeup of our engineering team, Vercel really scaled with our needs so well."The team builds its physician-facing web application with the . When engineers push changes to a development branch, Vercel , giving them a link they can use for live demos and share with colleagues to try new features. Pushing or merging into the production branch then triggers the production build and deployment. If a release needs reverting, the team can .Next.js frameworkbuilds and deploys a previewroll back to a previous deploymentThat workflow lets the team release multiple times a day, with each change becoming available to a physician audience that Kush thinks about whenever he ships something:Keeping that application available means handling demand the team can’t always anticipate. Andy was scrolling through Slack when he saw the message that OpenEvidence had gone viral on TikTok, reaching around two million views in under a week. He watched traffic climb and checked the logs. , and with no additional capacity to provision, he went back to his work.Response times stayed fast and error rates remained near zeroBeyond sudden spikes, the team has accommodated sustained growth without rebuilding the web application."Not once have I had to think, now that we have five times as many doctors, what's happening to page loads or time to first paint," Kush says. "The scaling has happened so naturally that we end up focusing on other things."As usage grew, VP of Engineering Micah Smith was watching compute costs. The team enabled  for its functions on Vercel, and Micah  alongside the wider infrastructure budget:Fluid computedescribed the result"We reduced our serverless spend by 90% while maintaining the same performance, and even as we've scaled up to 1000x growth, Vercel is less than 5% of our overall infra spend."Fluid compute lets multiple requests share a running function instance, so it can handle other work while a request waits for another service, such as a database or an AI backend, to respond. With , that waiting time doesn’t incur CPU charges, though memory remains billed while requests are in progress.Active CPU pricingTake Home, OpenEvidence’s first patient-facing application, lets a doctor translate a clinical answer into plain language and share it with a patient, who logs in to review and save the evidence. Clinical-trial matching is also part of the application’s planned direction.To support this expansion, the team uses a pattern established through dozens of early proofs of concept, each deployed as its own  with a custom domain. Stakeholders could open those applications and test the workflows for themselves.
